Box 1. Key findings of the Policy Survey on School Education in the Digital Age 

The Policy Survey on School Education in the Digital Age provides a n overview of education systems’ 

policy approaches to the digital transformation of school education in 2025. Several key findings emerge from the survey: 

• Digital education now assumes a prominent position in countries’ central education policy strategies. The implementation of these strategies is increasingly supported by funding and accountability mechanisms and many jurisdictions require schools to develop corresponding digital strategies. While most central strategies cover digital infrastructure and teachers’ 

capacity, fewer include initiatives or goals related to artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies. 

• Binding regulations on the use of digital resources in schools remain the exception and most jurisdictions rely on non-binding guidelines, particularly for emerging technologies like AI. While privacy and data protection are regulated across all jurisdictions, approaches to enforcement and implementation support vary. Around half of jurisdictions have processes in place to certify the quality or safety of digital education resources. 

• The funding and procurement of digital education resources tends to be complex, often involving multiple levels of administration and different funding mechanisms for different types of goods and services. In many systems, schools share some responsibility for the procurement of digital devices or software and central authorities use a range of approaches to support them by providing guidance, negotiating with suppliers or setting purchasing criteria. 

• Many jurisdictions allow for local flexibility to ensure students' access to digital devices and give sub-central authorities or schools the discretion to select appropriate strategies. Although 1:1-policies, which provide all students in need with a portable device, appear to be widespread (particularly at the secondary level), not all systems have a centrally defined strategy to ensure that disadvantaged students have access to a digital device for learning. 

• The use of digital resources is an integral part of many initial teacher education (ITE) programmes, but whether and how it is integrated is often at the discretion of ITE institutions. While only a few jurisdictions require teachers to participate in continuing professional learning (CPL) on digital technologies, most systems offer free learning opportunities. 

• The use of digital resources is now mentioned in many systems' professional standards for teachers. Of the jurisdictions with central appraisal or evaluation frameworks, around half also 

systematically considered teachers’ use of digital resources when evaluating their work ,although the systematic evaluation or certification of teachers' digital skills at the central level is not yet widespread. 

• The evaluation of the use of digital resources in schools remains limited, with only a third of jurisdictions systematically considering it in external school evaluations. More frequently, authorities rely on schools to evaluate their own use of digital resources and just under half of jurisdictions have made this a formal part of schools’ self-evaluation frameworks. 

• While most jurisdictions report that they assess the impact of their digital education policies on student outcomes, evaluations primarily focus on students' digital skills. Less attention is paid to student outcomes like cognitive skills, their well-being, or socio-emotional skills. 

• Many countries have updated their school curricula to integrate digital skills and learning contents, but only a few have included interactive features in their digital curricula so far. Although the importance of digital skills is widely recognised, their systematic assessment remains limited. Only a minority of jurisdictions are covering them in school-based assessments or central examinations.  11

They cover jurisdictions’ digital education strategies  (Section 1); the adaptation of  pedagogical approaches, curricula and assessments to digital education (Section 2); the governance, guidance and regulation of digital education (Section 3); funding and procurement (Section 4); digital infrastructure and innovation (Section 5); building capacity for digital education (Section 6); the alignment of human resource policies with digital education (Section 7); and instruments to monitor and evaluate digital education and its impact on students (Section 8). 1. Strategic visions and policy co-ordination for digital education 

Reaping the benefits of digital technology to advance quality, equity and efficiency in education systems requires  a co-ordinated and strategic approach, spanning multiple policy domains and  operating at different levels of intervention, from the central to the school level. A clear strategic vision can provide the foundation for successful reforms in this area, serving as a basis to articulate goals, to develop digital education policies that are aligned with broader educational and societal objectives, and to co-ordinate them across sectors and levels of governance. This section describes how central-level strategies 4 and associated instruments are used in participating jurisdictions to shape the digital transformation of their school systems and to co-ordinate digital education policies. 

Many school systems have developed central-level strategies for digital education policy in recent years 

Previous OECD analyses from 2022 showed that many OECD and EU countries had recently updated or were in the process of revising their education strategies to account for the changing role of digital education technologies since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) (OECD, 2023, p. 42 [2] ). Since then, the share of countries developing strategies specifically dedicated to digital education has only increased. 

The results of the Policy Survey show that all of the participating systems are addressing digital education in their high-level strategic documents guiding education reforms – either in dedicated digital education strategies or in broader strategies covering the sector. The majority of responding jurisdictions (23 of 37 [62%]) have a central-level strategy specifically dedicated to digital education ( Figure 1.1 ). In another 10

Most digital education strategies cover technological infrastructure and capacity building while emerging technologies are addressed in more limited ways 

Digital education strategies vary in the range of thematic areas they cover as well as the depth and level of specificity with which they are addressed. At the start of the 2020s, many OECD countries’ d igital education strategies focused on infrastructure and learning environments, fostering digital competency and bridging digital divides (van der Vlies, 2020 [3] ). Improving access to high-speed Internet connections and digital devices in education institutions was at the heart of many national strategies, while advanced technologies, such as AI, were rarely addressed in detail (OECD, 2023, p. 44 [2] ). 

In the intervening years, most countries have addressed the rise of AI and other emerging technologies in their education strategies, even though the majority of strategies do not feature specific initiatives or goals on the topic. Responses to the Policy Survey highlight which policy areas are not only mentioned in most digital education strategies but that are also the subject of specific strategic initiatives in around two thirds of the responding jurisdictions. This includes digital education infrastructure (incl. access to fast and reliable Internet, digital devices and software for schools), the effective use of digital technologies (incl. the 

use of digital resources for teaching and teachers’ capacity to integrate them), and the adaptation of curricula to foster students’ digital skills, their well-being and their safety in digital environments (Figure 1.2 ). Other thematic areas that are not only mentioned, but also linked to specific initiatives in a significant number of strategies, include standard-setting and quality assurance for digital education, technical support staff for schools, stimulating innovation in the EdTech sector (9 systems respectively). By contrast, even though the use of AI in education is mentioned in the strategies of 26 of the 32 responding jurisdictions (81%), only 8 strategies (25%) contain specific initiatives and 6 strategies (19%) include time-bound goals on the topic ( Figure 1.2 ).  13

Digital education strategies are increasingly supported by funding, implementation and accountability mechanisms 

To serve as an effective vehicle for reform, central strategies for digital education can be linked to a number of mechanisms and instruments designed to facilitate the implementation of associated policies. This includes, for example, well-structured action plans that include time-bound goals and assign responsibilities among key actors, designated budgets and funding mechanisms, as well as robust frameworks to monitor and evaluate the strategy’s progress (OECD, 2023, p. 44 [2] ). All 31 of the responding jurisdictions with relevant central strategies covering digital education had linked them to one or more such instruments. 

Typically, digital education strategies were linked to a designated implementation budget (23 systems [74%]), included time-bound goals (24 systems [77%]) and assigned responsibilities for implementation (26 systems [84%]). While 24 of 31 (77%) systems linked their strategies to instruments designed to monitoring their implementation (e.g. regular progress reviews), only 19 (61%) included indicators to measure the strategies’ implementation progress and outcomes and only 17 (55%) included formal processes to evaluate their outcomes ( Figure 1.3 ). 14 

2. Adapting pedagogical approaches, curricula and assessments for digital education 

Public authorities can use a range of policy levers to promote the effective use of digital technologies for teaching and learning. This section describes initiatives that participating jurisdictions use to guide teachers ’ effective use of digital resources or to promote peer learning on the selection and use of digital technologies. It also examines how curricula and assessment frameworks are being adapted to account 

for the use of digital technologies in the classroom and to promote students’ digital skills. 

Most systems provide central support for teachers’ effective use of digital resources 

Although the COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated teachers’ take -up of digital technologies, not all of them are able to use their full potential to enable a more individualised, efficient or responsive form of teaching and learning (OECD, 2023, p. 62 [2] ). Although teachers and school leaders tend to have significant pedagogical autonomy in deciding when and how to use digital education resources, central education authorities can play an important role in promoting their effective integration.  All of the 37 jurisdictions responding to the Policy Survey reported having some central initiatives in place to support teachers in their use of digital resources ( Figure 2.1 ). 

For example, 25 systems (68%) provide teachers with guidance on good practices for the use of digital resources and 24 systems (65%) support teachers’ p eer-to-peer training on the subject.  Many central authorities have also invested in platforms that allow educators to access digital teaching materials and adapt them to their needs. Specifically,  32 systems (86%) had invested in online platforms that provide digital education content for teachers and 25 systems (68%) reported operating interactive platforms that allow teachers to share digital education content with peers. In light of recent advances in artificial intelligence, 17 systems (46%) also reported having launched initiatives on the use of AI for teaching (Figure 2.1 ). 16 

Curricula are increasingly adapted to the use of digital education resources 

Governments across the OECD recognise the importance of developing students’ digital skills and data

Many countries have therefore engaged in reforms to update their school curricula by integrating digital skills and content related to digital technologies (OECD, 2020 [4] ) (see  Annex Table 2.1 ). At the same time, curricula are increasingly adapted to students’ and teachers’ use of digital technologies in the learning process. The results of the Policy Survey show that 23 of 37 responding jurisdictions (62%) include guidelines on students’ use of digital devices in their curricula and 15 systems (41%) include links to digital textbooks or other digital education content ( Figure 2.2 ). 

Most jurisdictions make curriculum documents available online to facilitate the access for teachers, students and other stakeholders. These digital curricula tend to be in static formats (e.g. PDF). However, an increasing number of school systems embrace the potential of making curriculum documents more interactive,  for example by enabling teachers to filter and to access education contents across grades and subjects or by assisting users in designing lessons in line with curriculum goals . Students’ digital skills are not systematically assessed in many countries 

The importance of developing students’ digital skills is acknowledged in the curricula of all responding jurisdictions and teaching digital skills is either recommended or mandated in all of them (in most cases transversally, across a number of compulsory subjects) (see  Annex Table 2.1 ). 3. Governance, guidance and regulation for digital education 

This section covers the governance of digital education. In more than half of the jurisdictions responding to the Policy Survey (24 of 37 [65%]), primary responsibility for regulating the use of digital education resources is shared across multiple levels of administration. Both schools and central authorities were reported as holding key responsibilities in this domain in 25 jurisdictions (68%) respectively (see  Annex Table 3.1 ). Given this important role played by central authorities, the following sections address central-level guidance and regulatory frameworks designed to support the effective use of digital resources. They also cover central provisions aiming to ensure privacy, data protection and the quality of digital resources in schools. 

Binding regulations concerning the use of digital resources in schools remain the exception, particularly for emerging technologies 

Central authorities dispose of different means to steer the use of digital resources in schools, including binding regulations as well as guidelines designed to inform practitioners’ decisions on the use of digital 

resources. Results from the Policy Survey show that the majority of the 37 responding jurisdictions provide guidelines addressing cyber security in education institutions (29 systems [78%] ), students’ well-being in digital environments (29 systems [78%] ) and students’ learning in digital environments (21 systems [57%]). Although less widespread, many jurisdictions also provide guidelines on the use of generative AI in the classroom (18 of 37 systems [49%]) and technical standards to improve interoperability (17 of 36 systems [47%]). By contrast, as of 2025, only 2 systems (Korea and Singapore) had issued guidelines on monitoring algorithmic bias – a concern that has increased over the last decade (Baker, Lee and Hawn, 2023 [5] )(Figure 3.1 ). So far, fewer systems have issued binding regulations affecting these areas. The domains that are most commonly regulated among the responding jurisdictions are cyber security in education institutions (13 systems [35%] ) and students’ well -being in digital environments (8 systems [22%]). Typically these binding regulations complement central guidelines on the same topics ( Figure 3.1 ).  19

While the protection of privacy and data in schools is regulated in all participating jurisdictions, support for its implementation varies 

The digital transformation has presented education institutions with new challenges concerning students’ 

information privacy as well as the security of their data and their activities online. All 37 responding jurisdictions reported having privacy and data protection regulations that apply to schools ( Figure 3.2 ). This reflects the heightened awareness surrounding the importance of protecting sensitive data and – in EU countries – the introduction of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which has strengthened

At the same time, the measures taken to support or accompany the implementation of privacy and data protection regulations very significantly across the responding jurisdictions. Most central authorities (in 30 of 37 systems [81%]) reported providing schools with guidance on the implementation of privacy and data protection measures or regulations. Where responsibilities for privacy and data protection in schools are centrally regulated, they tend to be entrusted to trained individuals. In 19 systems (51%), schools are obliged to assign responsibility to implement privacy and data protection measures to a trained member of staff. Around half of jurisdictions have processes to certify the quality or safety of digital education resources 

The certification of digital education resources or their providers can provide schools, teachers and other stakeholders with an effective means to identify safe and high-quality products while encouraging developers and suppliers to meet high standards. 4. Funding and procurement for digital education 

This section describes how responsibilities for purchasing digital resources are distributed, how central authorities support procurement processes and which mechanisms they use to fund the digital transformation of schools. Almost all jurisdictions participating in the Policy Survey reported having undertaken major public investments in digital education over the past five years. Investments in the digital education infrastructure tend to be complex, involving a mix of current and capital expenditure on resources ranging from broadband access and digital devices to learning software. Furthermore, responsibilities for the procurement of digital resources are often shared between multiple levels of administration and investments tend to involve funding obtained through more than one allocation mechanism (see  Annex Table 4.1 ). As a result of this complexity, comparative data on the extent of digital education investments and evidence of their efficiency remain limited (OECD, 2023, p. 113 [2] ). The results from the Policy Survey seek to provide an overview of international funding and procurement systems for digital resources in order to facilitate comparative analyses. 

Schools have some responsibility for procuring digital devices in many systems, typically drawing on funding allocated by central or sub-central authorities 

Results from the Policy Survey show that schools have some responsibility for procuring digital devices in 26 of 37 responding jurisdictions (70%). Sub-central authorities have some responsibility for the procurement of digital devices in almost as many systems (23 of 37 [62%]), and central authorities are responsible in 15 of 37 systems (41%). In around half of all responding jurisdictions (19 of 37 [51%]), the responsibility is shared between at least two levels of administration (i.e. schools, sub-central or central authorities). Among the 18 jurisdictions where a single level is responsible for procuring digital devices, the responsibility is most commonly assigned to schools (9 systems) and less frequently to sub-central or central authorities (5 and 4 systems respectively) (see  Annex Table 4.1 ). 5. Infrastructure and innovation for digital education 

Strengthening the digital education infrastructure and expanding access to high-speed Internet connections in schools, bridging digital divides and ensuring the availability of high-quality digital devices are central elements of many national strategies for digital education. This section considers the policy environment in which these efforts take place. It covers policies aimed at enhancing the quality and accessibility of the digital infrastructure, the types of digital resources that central authorities typically provide for schools (see  Annex Table 5.2 ), as well as strategies to promote EdTech innovation and the development of cutting-edge digital education tools. 

Students’ access to digital devices for learning is often organised at the sub-central level 

Results from PISA 2022 show that higher-performing school systems tend to have higher computer-to-student ratios, even after accounting for per capita GDP (OECD, 2023, pp. 409, Table II.B1.5.24 [6] ). Given the increasing use on digital devices for learning (both in schools and at home), providing students with access to digital devices has become an important condition for successful teaching and learning. The Policy Survey provides a more detailed picture of the policies that school systems use to widen access to digital devices for learning. 

At both the primary and upper secondary education levels, sub-central authorities or schools have discretion over how to ensure students’ access to digital devices in most responding jurisdictions (20 and 19 out of 37 respectively [54% and 51%]). Among the systems with centralised approaches at the primary level, most reported having a 1:1 policy, meaning that all students who need portable devices for learning 

receive a laptop or tablet to use in their school (7 systems [19%]) or both at school and at home (5 systems [14%]). 1:1 initiatives are similarly popular at the upper secondary level, although it is more common for 26 

5 systems (14%) reported that most upper secondary schools have a Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) policy, which was the case for only one system at the primary level. A small number of jurisdictions reported that students do not use portable devices in primary schools (6 systems [16%]) or upper secondary schools (4 systems [11%]), which suggests that students use desktop computers when working with digital devices at school and private devices when working at home. Finally, a significant share of jurisdiction reported

EdTech innovation, research and development is supported through a range of instruments in two thirds of jurisdictions 

The development and improvement of digital education resources is an important part of a strong digital education ecosystem. In addition to traditional  education stakeholders, many advances in this field are now driven by education technology (EdTech) companies. Public authorities can play an important role in connecting the work of the EdTech sector with that of education practitioners and bringing together actors from  government, research, industry, schools and other stakeholder groups to  set priorities and advance the effective use of digital tools in schools. Some governments have therefore started providing targeted support to encourage the development of digital education resources that are aligned with the sector ’spriorities or to foster collaborative forms of development (OECD, 2023, pp. 18, 319 [7] ). 

Evidence from the Policy Survey indicates that more than two thirds of responding jurisdictions (25 of 36 [69%]) use at least one form of targeted support to encourage EdTech innovation, research or developments (see  Annex Table 5.3 ).  The approach most widely used by central authorities (in 16 systems [44%]) is to commission the development of EdTech solutions. 13 systems (36%) reported carrying out R&D or developing EdTech through public agencies and providing competitive grants respectively. 12 jurisdictions (33%) also reported  providing monetary incentives, either for the development of digital education content, of education software or of AI-based EdTech solutions. 6. Capacity building for digital education 

Realising the potential of digital technologies to enhance teaching and learning requires people who are prepared, motivated and empowered to put digital resources to effective use. This section covers policies designed to build capacity for digital education among actors at all levels of the education system, including teachers, school leaders and parents . The section considers teachers’ initial education and continuing professional learning as well as structural supports aimed at encouraging the take-up of digital education technologies in schools. It also addresses efforts to support school leaders and parents in contributing to the digital transformation of education. 

The use of digital resources is now an integral part of many ITE programmes, but whether and how it is integrated is often at the discretion of institutions 

Preparing teachers for the effective use of digital education technologies is a key component of many 

education systems’ digital strategies. Modernising ITE programmes plays an important role in this process and results from TALIS indicate that recent teacher cohorts are more likely to have received training in the use of information and communication technology (ICT) than their more experienced peers (OECD, 2019, p. 207 [8] ). Nevertheless, prospective teachers’ exposure to effective digital pedagogies is not universal in 

all countries. Public authorities in some systems play a role in steering the content of ITE programmes, for example by prescribing core contents for ITE programmes  through accreditation criteria or by developing central learning goals or curricula for ITE programmes. 

In the Policy Survey, just under half of the jurisdictions (16 of 35 [46%]) reported that the use of digital resources is a mandatory component for all ITE programmes aimed at general subject teachers in lower  29

7. Human resource policies for digital education 

Attracting and retaining effective teachers remains an important challenge for many countries and economies and the strategies needed to accomplish this goal must be adapted to the digital age. 5 Career structures, professional standards and appraisal systems can provide education professionals with incentives to enhance their digital skills, to integrate new technologies into their practice and to experiment with innovative digital teaching methods.  This section  explores how human resource policies for teachers, school leaders and other school staff can be adapted to account for the digital transformation of their work. It focuses on the adaptation of professional standards and appraisal systems to the use of digital technologies as well as the creation of dedicated staff positions with responsibilities for the use or maintenance of digital resources in schools. 

While teachers’ work with digital resources is reflected in many countries’ professional 

standards, most appraisal systems are not designed to reward their effective use 

Including references to digital competencies or the use of digital technologies in professional teaching standards and evaluation frameworks can incentivise teachers to continue developing their professional practices. It can also provide recognition for teachers who use digital technologies in particularly innovative and effective ways in the classroom (OECD, 2023, p. 203 [2] ). As education authorities and stakeholders adapt teacher policies to the changing realities of the classroom, many reflect on the evolving role of educators and what it means to be an effective teacher in the digital age.  Among the 29 jurisdictions with central  professional standards or formal role descriptions for teachers (at ISCED 2), 21 (72%) reported that they already include  references to the use of digital resources. However, among the 21 jurisdictions with central appraisal or evaluation frameworks, fewer than half (11 systems [52%]) systematically consider teach ers’ use of digital resources when evaluating their work ( Figure 7.1 ). 8. Monitoring and evaluation for digital education 

Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms are important elements of any successful digital education policy ecosystem. Countries draw on a diverse range of approaches to evaluate the performance of students, teachers, school leaders, schools and the education system as a whole. Many school systems use a combination of school self-evaluations, external school evaluations, national student examinations, administrative data collections and appraisal processes. These instruments can be used to gain a better 

understanding of students’ learning progress, to provide information to parents and other stakeholders, or to improve school leadership and teaching practices (OECD, 2013, p. 17 [12] ). This section addresses 

central authorities’ strategies to monitor the state of digitalisation in their education systems and to evaluate the impact of their digital education policies. Results of the Policy Survey should be interpreted bearing in mind the significant heterogeneity of national quality assurance frameworks and practices. 

Important aspects of digital education in schools are not yet systematically evaluated 

Internal and external evaluation mechanisms at the school level can play an important role in enhancing the use of digital technologies for teaching, learning and management (OECD, 2023, p. 94 [2] ). Fewer than half of the jurisdictions responding to the Policy Survey (17 of 37 systems [46%]) reported using external school evaluations (i.e. inspections or external reviews) to collect information related to digital education systematically. The topics that are most frequently monitored through external evaluations are the u se of digital resources in schools and their access to fast and reliable Internet (13 systems [35%], respectively), as well as the availability and quality of digital devices in schools (12 systems [32%]).  10 systems (27%) reported that external school evaluations are used to monitor teachers ’ skills for incorporating digital 

resources into teaching and 5 systems (14%) reported monitoring the availability of technical support staff (Figure 8.1 ).  37

A slightly larger share of responding jurisdictions (20 of 37 [54%]) has embedded aspects of digital 

education in schools’ self -evaluation frameworks  (see  Annex Table 8.1 ).  Particularly the use of digital 

resources and teachers’ digital skills are more frequently covered by schools’ self-evaluations (in 17 and 14 systems respectively [46% and 28%]), than by external reviews or inspections. The availability and quality of digital devices is the subject of schools’ self -evaluations in 14 systems (38%) and the availability of technical support staff in 9 systems (24%) . By contrast, schools’ a ccess to fast and reliable Internet is more frequently monitored through external evaluations than self-evaluations (10 systems [27%]) (Figure 8.1 ).

The impact of digital education policies is evaluated for a narrow set of student outcomes, with most countries focusing on digital skills 

The use of digital education technologies in schools is not an end in itself but should serve to improve the quality of teaching and learning. It should be aligned with promoting system-wide goals like equity, inclusion or efficiency and ultimately improve outcomes for students. If the right conditions are in place to enable their effective use, digital education technologies can enhance a range of student outcomes, including their cognitive skills and digital literacy, their socio-emotional skills and well-being as well as their labour market and social outcomes (OECD, 2023, p. 24 [2] ). Conversely, there are justified concerns that the inadequate use of digital technologies in the classroom could do more harm than good. Evaluating the impact of digital education policies is therefore critical to assess their effectiveness and to make adjustments where needed. 

Responses to the Policy Survey suggest that more than two thirds of the responding jurisdictions (23 of 36 [64%]) systematically evaluate the impact of digital education on student outcomes (see  Annex Table 8.2 ). However, the range of outcomes they consider is relatively narrow. 19 of 36 jurisdictions (53%) evaluate 

the impact of digital education policies on students’ digital skills and 6 do so exclusively. The impact on 

students' subject competency and content knowledge is evaluated less frequently (in 11 of 36 systems [33%]), as is the case for students' well-being and ability to navigate digital risks (9 of 35 systems [26%]), 38 

their cognitive skills (8 of 35 systems [23%]) and their social and emotional skills (7 of 35 systems [20%]) (Figure 8.2 ).  Jurisdictions reported using a diverse range of methods to evaluate the impact of digital education policies. Many of them are observational and not designed to identify causal effects, for example 

comparing students’ achievement in PISA across schools that make different use of digital technologies. Due to diversity of methods used, the practices reported by jurisdictions’ may not be directly comparable.

# Abstract 

The Policy Survey on School Education in the Digital Age collected comparative information on the digital education policies in OECD member and partner countries. 37 jurisdictions participated, providing information on the state of their digital education policy ecosystem in January 2025. The survey results cover central-level policies across a range of domains: Central strategies and policy co-ordination for digital education; governance and regulation ; the adaptation of  pedagogical approaches, curricula and assessments to digital education; funding and procurement of digital resources; digital infrastructure and innovation; building educators and other stakeholders’ digital capacity; aligning h uman resource policies with digital education; and frameworks to monitor and evaluate digital education and its impact on students. The main text of the working paper provides an overview of key findings related to each of these domains. 

Annex A  presents the complete survey results and individual jurisdictions’ responses in comparative tables. Taken together, the results of the Policy Survey are intended to strengthen the evidence base on digital education policies, facilitate international peer learning and support public authorities in developing policies and strategies for the successful digital transformation of school education.  5

Background 

Digital technologies have become a key resource for OECD education and training systems. If used effectively, they promise to transform teaching and learning practices and to advance quality, equity and efficiency in education. Investment in education technology has surged worldwide over the past decade and digital education technologies increasingly permeate schools and classrooms. At the same time, access to high-quality digital technologies remains partial and unequally distributed in many education systems and their use often falls short of genuinely transforming teaching and learning practices. Enabling digital education policies are therefore needed for school systems to make effective use of digital technologies, to reap their full potential and to ensure that the teaching profession is ready for the digital age. 

The  unprecedented increase in the use of digital education resources during the  COVID-19 pandemic and the rapid progress in generative artificial intelligence in recent years have made it a top priority for governments to review and adapt policies to effectively and equitably prepare schools for the digital age. The OECD umbrella project Resourcing School Education: Policies for the Digital Transformation of Education and Future-Readiness of Teachers was launched in 2023 in order to  collect comparative, qualitative data to support  this process and to inform the development of system-level digital education policies  (OECD, 2025 [1] ). The Policy Survey on School Education in the Digital Age (hereafter “the Policy Survey”) and its associated outputs are designed to inform this work and to strengthen the project’s 

comparative evidence base on digital education policies. This working paper provides a first descriptive 

overview of the Policy Survey’s results, which will be subject to more in-depth analyses carried out by the 

Resourcing School Education  project and will inform its country-specific work going forward. 

Thematic coverage and analytical framework 

The Policy Survey covers two of the umbrella project’s thematic strands:  Strand 1 ( “Policies for the digital transformation of school education ”) and Strand 2 ( “Policies for a future-ready teaching profession in the digital age ”).  The main text of this working paper focuses on Strand 1, presenting a descriptive summary of the survey results, highlighting key findings related to each of the survey’s thematic areas. Comparative tables with the complete survey data and individual juris dictions’ responses – including those on teacher shortages and career structures under Strand 2 – are presented in  Annex A . A summary of the survey’s 

main findings is provided in  Box 1 . Throughout the working paper, the Policy Survey results are presented 

in line with the project’s analytical framework (see  Figure 1 ), which covers the following eight dimensions of Strand 1 as well as Strand 2: 

• Dimension 1: Strategic visions and policy co-ordination 

• Dimension 2: Adapting pedagogical approaches, curricula and assessments 

• Dimension 3: Governance, guidance and regulation

The education systems that participated in the Policy Survey have taken different approaches to the digital transformation of schools and this working paper presents them in a comparative way. Nevertheless, the survey results need to be interpreted in the context of the diversity of the participating jurisdictions ’

education systems, for example their different degrees of centralisation and variations in the locus of decision making. Respondents were asked to provide information pertaining to their highest level of government, i.e. the central level of government or the highest level of decision making in the case of  sub-national entities. For  policy areas that are not under the responsibility of the respective highest levels of government, respondents were encouraged to report the most common policies implemented at lower levels of government and to highlight variations in the table notes. 

Since the results of the Policy Survey reflect system-level policy frameworks, it is also important to bear in mind that their expression may vary within jurisdictions at the local level. Central policies and regulations may be subject to differential implementation or interpretation, which may lead to some degree of heterogeneity across local units and schools, or discrepancies between system-level frameworks and the experience of education professionals on the ground. As for any system-level data collection, it is therefore important to com plement and triangulate the Policy Survey’s results with additional data sources , which the  Resourcing School Education  project will do in future analytical outputs.  9

Participation 

The survey was completed by 37 jurisdictions (26 OECD member countries, 7 sub-national entities 1 and 4 non-member economies): Austria, Chile, Colombia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Israel, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Korea, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, New South Wales (NSW) in Australia, the Flemish Community of Belgium, the French Community of Belgium, England (United Kingdom), Northern Ireland (UK), Scotland (UK), Wales (UK), Bulgaria, Croatia, Romania and Singapore.  Throughout this document, the terms “jurisdictions” and “systems” are used interchangeably to 

refer to the survey respondents. 

Survey administration 

The results presented in this document reflect the digital education policies of participating jurisdictions in January 2025. The OECD Secretariat presented a draft of the survey questionnaire at an informal meeting of the Group of National Experts on School Resources (GNE-SR) on 13 September 2023. The survey was revised based on the feedback received and shared with jurisdictions in October 2023. The OECD Secretariat received responses over the course of the first half of 2024 and validated them from November 2024 to January 2025, including any updates on recent policy developments. The survey questions were presented in fixed-response format with the option to provide additional information to clarify or add nuance to responses in open-ended questions and comment fields. 2 One response per (national or sub-national) education system was requested. 

Scope and definitions 

The survey covers policies concerning public school and government-dependent private schools at the primary and secondary levels of education. Unless otherwise specified, responses refer to ISCED 3 levels 1-3 and notable differences across levels of education in individual jurisdictions are explained in the table notes. Where policies differed between general education and technical and vocational education and training (TVET), respondents were asked to report on the policies applicable to general education and to describe policies applicable to TVET in the table notes. 

Building on the terminology used in the OECD Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 and the OECD Teaching and Learning International Study (TALIS) 2024, the Policy Survey uses the 

term “digital resources” to refer to : 1) d igital devices or “hardware” (computers, table ts, smartphones, 3D printers, etc.), 2) software (programmes, apps, communication tools, educational learning tools, etc.) and 

3)  online resources and digital education content (websites, web portals, digital textbooks, etc.).  Definitions of other key terms are provided in notes under the relevant tables in  Annex A . Please note that the definitions are chosen in the context of this survey and may not reflect those used in other OECD data collections.

Box 1. Key findings of the Policy Survey on School Education in the Digital Age 

The Policy Survey on School Education in the Digital Age provides a n overview of education systems’ 

policy approaches to the digital transformation of school education in 2025. Several key findings emerge from the survey: 

• Digital education now assumes a prominent position in countries’ central education policy strategies. The implementation of these strategies is increasingly supported by funding and accountability mechanisms and many jurisdictions require schools to develop corresponding digital strategies. While most central strategies cover digital infrastructure and teachers’ 

capacity, fewer include initiatives or goals related to artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies. 

• Binding regulations on the use of digital resources in schools remain the exception and most jurisdictions rely on non-binding guidelines, particularly for emerging technologies like AI. While privacy and data protection are regulated across all jurisdictions, approaches to enforcement and implementation support vary. Around half of jurisdictions have processes in place to certify the quality or safety of digital education resources. 

• The funding and procurement of digital education resources tends to be complex, often involving multiple levels of administration and different funding mechanisms for different types of goods and services. In many systems, schools share some responsibility for the procurement of digital devices or software and central authorities use a range of approaches to support them by providing guidance, negotiating with suppliers or setting purchasing criteria. 

• Many jurisdictions allow for local flexibility to ensure students' access to digital devices and give sub-central authorities or schools the discretion to select appropriate strategies. Although 1:1-policies, which provide all students in need with a portable device, appear to be widespread (particularly at the secondary level), not all systems have a centrally defined strategy to ensure that disadvantaged students have access to a digital device for learning. 

• The use of digital resources is an integral part of many initial teacher education (ITE) programmes, but whether and how it is integrated is often at the discretion of ITE institutions. While only a few jurisdictions require teachers to participate in continuing professional learning (CPL) on digital technologies, most systems offer free learning opportunities. 

• The use of digital resources is now mentioned in many systems' professional standards for teachers. Of the jurisdictions with central appraisal or evaluation frameworks, around half also 

systematically considered teachers’ use of digital resources when evaluating their work ,although the systematic evaluation or certification of teachers' digital skills at the central level is not yet widespread. 

• The evaluation of the use of digital resources in schools remains limited, with only a third of jurisdictions systematically considering it in external school evaluations. More frequently, authorities rely on schools to evaluate their own use of digital resources and just under half of jurisdictions have made this a formal part of schools’ self-evaluation frameworks. 

• While most jurisdictions report that they assess the impact of their digital education policies on student outcomes, evaluations primarily focus on students' digital skills. Less attention is paid to student outcomes like cognitive skills, their well-being, or socio-emotional skills. 

• Many countries have updated their school curricula to integrate digital skills and learning contents, but only a few have included interactive features in their digital curricula so far. Although the importance of digital skills is widely recognised, their systematic assessment remains limited. Only a minority of jurisdictions are covering them in school-based assessments or central examinations.  11

1. Strategic visions and policy co-ordination for digital education 

Reaping the benefits of digital technology to advance quality, equity and efficiency in education systems requires  a co-ordinated and strategic approach, spanning multiple policy domains and  operating at different levels of intervention, from the central to the school level. A clear strategic vision can provide the foundation for successful reforms in this area, serving as a basis to articulate goals, to develop digital education policies that are aligned with broader educational and societal objectives, and to co-ordinate them across sectors and levels of governance. This section describes how central-level strategies 4 and associated instruments are used in participating jurisdictions to shape the digital transformation of their school systems and to co-ordinate digital education policies. 

Many school systems have developed central-level strategies for digital education policy in recent years 

Previous OECD analyses from 2022 showed that many OECD and EU countries had recently updated or were in the process of revising their education strategies to account for the changing role of digital education technologies since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) (OECD, 2023, p. 42 [2] ). Since then, the share of countries developing strategies specifically dedicated to digital education has only increased. 

The results of the Policy Survey show that all of the participating systems are addressing digital education in their high-level strategic documents guiding education reforms – either in dedicated digital education strategies or in broader strategies covering the sector. The majority of responding jurisdictions (23 of 37 [62%]) have a central-level strategy specifically dedicated to digital education ( Figure 1.1 ). In another 10

Most digital education strategies cover technological infrastructure and capacity building while emerging technologies are addressed in more limited ways 

Digital education strategies vary in the range of thematic areas they cover as well as the depth and level of specificity with which they are addressed. At the start of the 2020s, many OECD countries’ d igital education strategies focused on infrastructure and learning environments, fostering digital competency and bridging digital divides (van der Vlies, 2020 [3] ). Improving access to high-speed Internet connections and digital devices in education institutions was at the heart of many national strategies, while advanced technologies, such as AI, were rarely addressed in detail (OECD, 2023, p. 44 [2] ). 

In the intervening years, most countries have addressed the rise of AI and other emerging technologies in their education strategies, even though the majority of strategies do not feature specific initiatives or goals on the topic. Responses to the Policy Survey highlight which policy areas are not only mentioned in most digital education strategies but that are also the subject of specific strategic initiatives in around two thirds of the responding jurisdictions. This includes digital education infrastructure (incl. access to fast and reliable Internet, digital devices and software for schools), the effective use of digital technologies (incl. the 

use of digital resources for teaching and teachers’ capacity to integrate them), and the adaptation of curricula to foster students’ digital skills, their well-being and their safety in digital environments (Figure 1.2 ). Other thematic areas that are not only mentioned, but also linked to specific initiatives in a significant number of strategies, include standard-setting and quality assurance for digital education, technical support staff for schools, stimulating innovation in the EdTech sector (9 systems respectively). By contrast, even though the use of AI in education is mentioned in the strategies of 26 of the 32 responding jurisdictions (81%), only 8 strategies (25%) contain specific initiatives and 6 strategies (19%) include time-bound goals on the topic ( Figure 1.2 ).  13

Digital education strategies are increasingly supported by funding, implementation and accountability mechanisms 

To serve as an effective vehicle for reform, central strategies for digital education can be linked to a number of mechanisms and instruments designed to facilitate the implementation of associated policies. This includes, for example, well-structured action plans that include time-bound goals and assign responsibilities among key actors, designated budgets and funding mechanisms, as well as robust frameworks to monitor and evaluate the strategy’s progress (OECD, 2023, p. 44 [2] ). All 31 of the responding jurisdictions with relevant central strategies covering digital education had linked them to one or more such instruments. 

Typically, digital education strategies were linked to a designated implementation budget (23 systems [74%]), included time-bound goals (24 systems [77%]) and assigned responsibilities for implementation (26 systems [84%]). While 24 of 31 (77%) systems linked their strategies to instruments designed to monitoring their implementation (e.g. regular progress reviews), only 19 (61%) included indicators to measure the strategies’ implementation progress and outcomes and only 17 (55%) included formal processes to evaluate their outcomes ( Figure 1.3 ). 14 

Schools in many education systems are required to develop plans or strategies addressing digital education 

In most OECD countries, responsibilities for decisions concerning the use of digital education resources are shared between actors across multiple levels of administration and schools bear some responsibility for regulating the use of digital resources in nearly all systems (see  Annex Table 3.1 ). A strategic approach to digitalisation is therefore not only needed at the central level, but also on the part of school leaders. Responses to the Policy Survey suggest that the great majority of responding jurisdictions require schools to engage in strategic reflections on their approach to digitalisation. 7 of 37 (19%) systems require schools to develop dedicated plans or strategies concerning digital education. An additional 15 of 37 (41%) systems require schools to cover the use of digital resources for teaching in more general plans or strategies they develop  (Figure 1.4 ).  15

2. Adapting pedagogical approaches, curricula and assessments for digital education 

Public authorities can use a range of policy levers to promote the effective use of digital technologies for teaching and learning. This section describes initiatives that participating jurisdictions use to guide teachers ’ effective use of digital resources or to promote peer learning on the selection and use of digital technologies. It also examines how curricula and assessment frameworks are being adapted to account 

for the use of digital technologies in the classroom and to promote students’ digital skills. 

Most systems provide central support for teachers’ effective use of digital resources 

Although the COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated teachers’ take -up of digital technologies, not all of them are able to use their full potential to enable a more individualised, efficient or responsive form of teaching and learning (OECD, 2023, p. 62 [2] ). Although teachers and school leaders tend to have significant pedagogical autonomy in deciding when and how to use digital education resources, central education authorities can play an important role in promoting their effective integration.  All of the 37 jurisdictions responding to the Policy Survey reported having some central initiatives in place to support teachers in their use of digital resources ( Figure 2.1 ). 

For example, 25 systems (68%) provide teachers with guidance on good practices for the use of digital resources and 24 systems (65%) support teachers’ p eer-to-peer training on the subject.  Many central authorities have also invested in platforms that allow educators to access digital teaching materials and adapt them to their needs. Specifically,  32 systems (86%) had invested in online platforms that provide digital education content for teachers and 25 systems (68%) reported operating interactive platforms that allow teachers to share digital education content with peers. In light of recent advances in artificial intelligence, 17 systems (46%) also reported having launched initiatives on the use of AI for teaching (Figure 2.1 ). 16 

Curricula are increasingly adapted to the use of digital education resources 

Governments across the OECD recognise the importance of developing students’ digital skills and data 

literacy to enable them to thrive in the 21st century. Many countries have therefore engaged in reforms to update their school curricula by integrating digital skills and content related to digital technologies (OECD, 2020 [4] ) (see  Annex Table 2.1 ). At the same time, curricula are increasingly adapted to students’ and teachers’ use of digital technologies in the learning process. The results of the Policy Survey show that 23 of 37 responding jurisdictions (62%) include guidelines on students’ use of digital devices in their curricula and 15 systems (41%) include links to digital textbooks or other digital education content ( Figure 2.2 ). 

Most jurisdictions make curriculum documents available online to facilitate the access for teachers, students and other stakeholders. These digital curricula tend to be in static formats (e.g. PDF). However, an increasing number of school systems embrace the potential of making curriculum documents more interactive,  for example by enabling teachers to filter and to access education contents across grades and subjects or by assisting users in designing lessons in line with curriculum goals . In the Policy Survey, 10 of 37 systems (27%) reported having integrated interactive elements in their curricula for lower secondary schools and several countries are in the process of making their curricula more interactive  (Figure 2.2 ).  17

Students’ digital skills are not systematically assessed in many countries 

The importance of developing students’ digital skills is acknowledged in the curricula of all responding jurisdictions and teaching digital skills is either recommended or mandated in all of them (in most cases transversally, across a number of compulsory subjects) (see  Annex Table 2.1 ). Nevertheless, students’ 

digital skills are not yet systematically assessed in many jurisdictions. Responses to the Policy Survey indicate that 14 of 36 responding jurisdictions (39%) assess digital skills through formative school-based assessments in lower secondary education. Even fewer systems reported doing so through summative school-based assessments (12 systems [33%]) or reported assessing digital skills in central examinations with stakes (France and Romania) ( Figure 2.3 ). By contrast, many jurisdictions reported assessing 

students’ digital skills using international surveys, such as the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) (23 systems [64%] in lower secondary education and 14 systems [38%] in primary and upper secondary education) or – particularly at the lower secondary level – through standardised examinations without stakes (12 systems [33%]) ( Figure 2.3 ). Excluding international surveys, just under a third of the responding jurisdictions (10 of 36 [28%]) do not systematically assess students’ digital skills. 18 

3. Governance, guidance and regulation for digital education 

This section covers the governance of digital education. In more than half of the jurisdictions responding to the Policy Survey (24 of 37 [65%]), primary responsibility for regulating the use of digital education resources is shared across multiple levels of administration. Both schools and central authorities were reported as holding key responsibilities in this domain in 25 jurisdictions (68%) respectively (see  Annex Table 3.1 ). Given this important role played by central authorities, the following sections address central-level guidance and regulatory frameworks designed to support the effective use of digital resources. They also cover central provisions aiming to ensure privacy, data protection and the quality of digital resources in schools. 

Binding regulations concerning the use of digital resources in schools remain the exception, particularly for emerging technologies 

Central authorities dispose of different means to steer the use of digital resources in schools, including binding regulations as well as guidelines designed to inform practitioners’ decisions on the use of digital 

resources. Results from the Policy Survey show that the majority of the 37 responding jurisdictions provide guidelines addressing cyber security in education institutions (29 systems [78%] ), students’ well-being in digital environments (29 systems [78%] ) and students’ learning in digital environments (21 systems [57%]). Although less widespread, many jurisdictions also provide guidelines on the use of generative AI in the classroom (18 of 37 systems [49%]) and technical standards to improve interoperability (17 of 36 systems [47%]). By contrast, as of 2025, only 2 systems (Korea and Singapore) had issued guidelines on monitoring algorithmic bias – a concern that has increased over the last decade (Baker, Lee and Hawn, 2023 [5] )(Figure 3.1 ). So far, fewer systems have issued binding regulations affecting these areas. The domains that are most commonly regulated among the responding jurisdictions are cyber security in education institutions (13 systems [35%] ) and students’ well -being in digital environments (8 systems [22%]). Typically these binding regulations complement central guidelines on the same topics ( Figure 3.1 ).  19

4. Funding and procurement for digital education 

This section describes how responsibilities for purchasing digital resources are distributed, how central authorities support procurement processes and which mechanisms they use to fund the digital transformation of schools. Almost all jurisdictions participating in the Policy Survey reported having undertaken major public investments in digital education over the past five years. Investments in the digital education infrastructure tend to be complex, involving a mix of current and capital expenditure on resources ranging from broadband access and digital devices to learning software. Furthermore, responsibilities for the procurement of digital resources are often shared between multiple levels of administration and investments tend to involve funding obtained through more than one allocation mechanism (see  Annex Table 4.1 ). As a result of this complexity, comparative data on the extent of digital education investments and evidence of their efficiency remain limited (OECD, 2023, p. 113 [2] ). The results from the Policy Survey seek to provide an overview of international funding and procurement systems for digital resources in order to facilitate comparative analyses. 

Schools have some responsibility for procuring digital devices in many systems, typically drawing on funding allocated by central or sub-central authorities 

Results from the Policy Survey show that schools have some responsibility for procuring digital devices in 26 of 37 responding jurisdictions (70%). Sub-central authorities have some responsibility for the procurement of digital devices in almost as many systems (23 of 37 [62%]), and central authorities are responsible in 15 of 37 systems (41%). In around half of all responding jurisdictions (19 of 37 [51%]), the responsibility is shared between at least two levels of administration (i.e. schools, sub-central or central authorities). Among the 18 jurisdictions where a single level is responsible for procuring digital devices, the responsibility is most commonly assigned to schools (9 systems) and less frequently to sub-central or central authorities (5 and 4 systems respectively) (see  Annex Table 4.1 ). Sub-central authorities procured digital devices using either their own funding (in 19 systems [51%]) or funding they receive from the central level (in 14 systems [38%]) ( Figure 4.1 ).

5. Infrastructure and innovation for digital education 

Strengthening the digital education infrastructure and expanding access to high-speed Internet connections in schools, bridging digital divides and ensuring the availability of high-quality digital devices are central elements of many national strategies for digital education. This section considers the policy environment in which these efforts take place. It covers policies aimed at enhancing the quality and accessibility of the digital infrastructure, the types of digital resources that central authorities typically provide for schools (see  Annex Table 5.2 ), as well as strategies to promote EdTech innovation and the development of cutting-edge digital education tools. 

Students’ access to digital devices for learning is often organised at the sub-central level 

Results from PISA 2022 show that higher-performing school systems tend to have higher computer-to-student ratios, even after accounting for per capita GDP (OECD, 2023, pp. 409, Table II.B1.5.24 [6] ). Given the increasing use on digital devices for learning (both in schools and at home), providing students with access to digital devices has become an important condition for successful teaching and learning. The Policy Survey provides a more detailed picture of the policies that school systems use to widen access to digital devices for learning. 

At both the primary and upper secondary education levels, sub-central authorities or schools have discretion over how to ensure students’ access to digital devices in most responding jurisdictions (20 and 19 out of 37 respectively [54% and 51%]). Among the systems with centralised approaches at the primary level, most reported having a 1:1 policy, meaning that all students who need portable devices for learning 

receive a laptop or tablet to use in their school (7 systems [19%]) or both at school and at home (5 systems [14%]). 1:1 initiatives are similarly popular at the upper secondary level, although it is more common for 26 

5 systems (14%) reported that most upper secondary schools have a Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) policy, which was the case for only one system at the primary level. A small number of jurisdictions reported that students do not use portable devices in primary schools (6 systems [16%]) or upper secondary schools (4 systems [11%]), which suggests that students use desktop computers when working with digital devices at school and private devices when working at home. Finally, a significant share of jurisdiction reported 

relying on “mixed strategies” to provide students with access to portable devices for learni ng (7 systems [19%] at the primary level and 11 systems [30%] at the upper secondary level) ( Figure 5.1 ). Such mixed strategies include, for example,  allowing students to use private devices and providing devices for students without access .

EdTech innovation, research and development is supported through a range of instruments in two thirds of jurisdictions 

The development and improvement of digital education resources is an important part of a strong digital education ecosystem. In addition to traditional  education stakeholders, many advances in this field are now driven by education technology (EdTech) companies. Public authorities can play an important role in connecting the work of the EdTech sector with that of education practitioners and bringing together actors from  government, research, industry, schools and other stakeholder groups to  set priorities and advance the effective use of digital tools in schools. Some governments have therefore started providing targeted support to encourage the development of digital education resources that are aligned with the sector ’spriorities or to foster collaborative forms of development (OECD, 2023, pp. 18, 319 [7] ). 

Evidence from the Policy Survey indicates that more than two thirds of responding jurisdictions (25 of 36 [69%]) use at least one form of targeted support to encourage EdTech innovation, research or developments (see  Annex Table 5.3 ).  The approach most widely used by central authorities (in 16 systems [44%]) is to commission the development of EdTech solutions. 13 systems (36%) reported carrying out R&D or developing EdTech through public agencies and providing competitive grants respectively. 12 jurisdictions (33%) also reported  providing monetary incentives, either for the development of digital education content, of education software or of AI-based EdTech solutions.  By contrast, providing tax credits to incentivise R&D on EdTech or investing directly in EdTech startups is less common, reported by only 4 and 7 jurisdictions respectively (11% and 19%) ( Figure 5.3 ). 28 

6. Capacity building for digital education 

Realising the potential of digital technologies to enhance teaching and learning requires people who are prepared, motivated and empowered to put digital resources to effective use. This section covers policies designed to build capacity for digital education among actors at all levels of the education system, including teachers, school leaders and parents . The section considers teachers’ initial education and continuing professional learning as well as structural supports aimed at encouraging the take-up of digital education technologies in schools. It also addresses efforts to support school leaders and parents in contributing to the digital transformation of education. 

The use of digital resources is now an integral part of many ITE programmes, but whether and how it is integrated is often at the discretion of institutions 

Preparing teachers for the effective use of digital education technologies is a key component of many 

education systems’ digital strategies. Modernising ITE programmes plays an important role in this process and results from TALIS indicate that recent teacher cohorts are more likely to have received training in the use of information and communication technology (ICT) than their more experienced peers (OECD, 2019, p. 207 [8] ). Nevertheless, prospective teachers’ exposure to effective digital pedagogies is not universal in 

all countries. Public authorities in some systems play a role in steering the content of ITE programmes, for example by prescribing core contents for ITE programmes  through accreditation criteria or by developing central learning goals or curricula for ITE programmes. 

In the Policy Survey, just under half of the jurisdictions (16 of 35 [46%]) reported that the use of digital resources is a mandatory component for all ITE programmes aimed at general subject teachers in lower  29

In another 17 systems (49%), integrating the  use of digital resources in teacher training programmes is at  the discretion of individual ITE institutions ( Figure 6.1 ). This relatively even divide between systems using central prescriptions and those with greater institutional autonomy held across levels of education, i.e. also for ITE programmes preparing primary and upper secondary education teachers (see  Annex Table 6.1 ).

7. Human resource policies for digital education 

Attracting and retaining effective teachers remains an important challenge for many countries and economies and the strategies needed to accomplish this goal must be adapted to the digital age. 5 Career structures, professional standards and appraisal systems can provide education professionals with incentives to enhance their digital skills, to integrate new technologies into their practice and to experiment with innovative digital teaching methods.  This section  explores how human resource policies for teachers, school leaders and other school staff can be adapted to account for the digital transformation of their work. It focuses on the adaptation of professional standards and appraisal systems to the use of digital technologies as well as the creation of dedicated staff positions with responsibilities for the use or maintenance of digital resources in schools. 

While teachers’ work with digital resources is reflected in many countries’ professional 

standards, most appraisal systems are not designed to reward their effective use 

Including references to digital competencies or the use of digital technologies in professional teaching standards and evaluation frameworks can incentivise teachers to continue developing their professional practices. It can also provide recognition for teachers who use digital technologies in particularly innovative and effective ways in the classroom (OECD, 2023, p. 203 [2] ). As education authorities and stakeholders adapt teacher policies to the changing realities of the classroom, many reflect on the evolving role of educators and what it means to be an effective teacher in the digital age.  Among the 29 jurisdictions with central  professional standards or formal role descriptions for teachers (at ISCED 2), 21 (72%) reported that they already include  references to the use of digital resources. However, among the 21 jurisdictions with central appraisal or evaluation frameworks, fewer than half (11 systems [52%]) systematically consider teach ers’ use of digital resources when evaluating their work ( Figure 7.1 ). Assigning responsibility for the maintenance of digital education resources is mostly at the discretion of schools or local authorities 

Digital software and devices require regular maintenance to ensure their continued security and functionality. In addition to specialised staff who can assist teachers in the pedagogical use of digital technologies, schools therefore need technical support to maintain their digital infrastructure and assist teachers or students with technical problems (OECD, 2023, p. 200 [2] ). Education systems across the OECD currently face significant gaps in the availability of technical assistance in schools. In PISA 2022, 41% of 15-year-old students attended schools whose principal reported having insufficiently qualified technical assistant staff, on average across the OECD (OECD, 2023, pp. 409, Table II.B1.5.32 [6] ). 

The Policy Survey provides an insight into the distribution of responsibilities for maintaining digital resources in schools. In most responding jurisdictions (27 of 37 systems [73%] at the lower secondary level), assigning responsibility for the maintenance of digital education resources is at the discretion of schools or local authorities. A minority of jurisdictions assign responsibility for the maintenance of digital resources at the central level. 8 systems (22%) reported that teachers exercise this role in a part-time or full-time capacity, 6 systems (16%) assign the responsibility to technical support staff (sometimes shared between multiple schools) and 4 systems (11%) assign maintenance responsibilities to external contractors. 10 systems (27%) have other arrangements or the responsibility for the maintenance of digital devices depends on school characteristics ( Figure 7.3 ).  In some school systems, more than one of these arrangements coexist (see  Annex Table 7.2  for a detailed overview). Differences across levels of education are relatively small. 36 

8. Monitoring and evaluation for digital education 

Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms are important elements of any successful digital education policy ecosystem. Countries draw on a diverse range of approaches to evaluate the performance of students, teachers, school leaders, schools and the education system as a whole. Many school systems use a combination of school self-evaluations, external school evaluations, national student examinations, administrative data collections and appraisal processes. These instruments can be used to gain a better 

understanding of students’ learning progress, to provide information to parents and other stakeholders, or to improve school leadership and teaching practices (OECD, 2013, p. 17 [12] ). This section addresses 

central authorities’ strategies to monitor the state of digitalisation in their education systems and to evaluate the impact of their digital education policies. Results of the Policy Survey should be interpreted bearing in mind the significant heterogeneity of national quality assurance frameworks and practices. 

Important aspects of digital education in schools are not yet systematically evaluated 

Internal and external evaluation mechanisms at the school level can play an important role in enhancing the use of digital technologies for teaching, learning and management (OECD, 2023, p. 94 [2] ). Fewer than half of the jurisdictions responding to the Policy Survey (17 of 37 systems [46%]) reported using external school evaluations (i.e. inspections or external reviews) to collect information related to digital education systematically. The topics that are most frequently monitored through external evaluations are the u se of digital resources in schools and their access to fast and reliable Internet (13 systems [35%], respectively), as well as the availability and quality of digital devices in schools (12 systems [32%]).  10 systems (27%) reported that external school evaluations are used to monitor teachers ’ skills for incorporating digital 

resources into teaching and 5 systems (14%) reported monitoring the availability of technical support staff (Figure 8.1 ).  37 

> Policies for the digital transformation of school education: Evidence from the Policy Survey on School Education in the Digital Age © OECD 2025

A slightly larger share of responding jurisdictions (20 of 37 [54%]) has embedded aspects of digital 

education in schools’ self -evaluation frameworks  (see  Annex Table 8.1 ).  Particularly the use of digital 

resources and teachers’ digital skills are more frequently covered by schools’ self-evaluations (in 17 and 14 systems respectively [46% and 28%]), than by external reviews or inspections. The availability and quality of digital devices is the subject of schools’ self -evaluations in 14 systems (38%) and the availability of technical support staff in 9 systems (24%) . By contrast, schools’ a ccess to fast and reliable Internet is more frequently monitored through external evaluations than self-evaluations (10 systems [27%]) (Figure 8.1 ).

The impact of digital education policies is evaluated for a narrow set of student outcomes, with most countries focusing on digital skills 

The use of digital education technologies in schools is not an end in itself but should serve to improve the quality of teaching and learning. It should be aligned with promoting system-wide goals like equity, inclusion or efficiency and ultimately improve outcomes for students. If the right conditions are in place to enable their effective use, digital education technologies can enhance a range of student outcomes, including their cognitive skills and digital literacy, their socio-emotional skills and well-being as well as their labour market and social outcomes (OECD, 2023, p. 24 [2] ). Conversely, there are justified concerns that the inadequate use of digital technologies in the classroom could do more harm than good. Evaluating the impact of digital education policies is therefore critical to assess their effectiveness and to make adjustments where needed. 

Responses to the Policy Survey suggest that more than two thirds of the responding jurisdictions (23 of 36 [64%]) systematically evaluate the impact of digital education on student outcomes (see  Annex Table 8.2 ). However, the range of outcomes they consider is relatively narrow. 19 of 36 jurisdictions (53%) evaluate 

the impact of digital education policies on students’ digital skills and 6 do so exclusively. The impact on 

students' subject competency and content knowledge is evaluated less frequently (in 11 of 36 systems [33%]), as is the case for students' well-being and ability to navigate digital risks (9 of 35 systems [26%]), 38 

their cognitive skills (8 of 35 systems [23%]) and their social and emotional skills (7 of 35 systems [20%]) (Figure 8.2 ).  Jurisdictions reported using a diverse range of methods to evaluate the impact of digital education policies. Many of them are observational and not designed to identify causal effects, for example 

comparing students’ achievement in PISA across schools that make different use of digital technologies. Due to diversity of methods used, the practices reported by jurisdictions’ may not be directly comparable.
