# 3.2 Key Findings 

3.2.1 The Internet as a Whole – Structural View 

Students’ conceptions of the internet as a whole ranged from vague and device-bound to more elaborate, network-based views. This chapter identifies seven main categories, ordered approximately by conceptual sophistication. While individual students frequently held multiple co-existing conceptions, this section presents each in isolation to highlight the dominant patterns across grade levels. These findings closely mirror international research, where similar progressions from device-bound to distributed-network views have been observed (e.g., Yan, 2005; Mertala, 2019; reviewed in Babari, Hielscher, Edelsbrunner, Conti, et al., 2023; Brom et al., 2023). 

The Internet Is Inside the Device 

Among younger students, the internet was often perceived as a component of the device itself or something inseparable from it. According to Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025), 19 (32.8%) out of 58 fourth-graders described it in this way: they struggled to distinguish the internet from the device and sometimes imagined a specific object or “chip” inside the device that stored and delivered all needed content. One student described it as “a green flash drive”: 

“[The internet] is controlled by a small flash drive, which has a huge amount of things inside … everything I [might] need to find … it’s black with green stripes … and that’s the internet, and that flash drive is the internet, and it’s in every device.” 

Grade 4, (Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025) Some of these students did not distinguish between local storage, application icons, and the internet as a broader system. Based on our typology of conceptions introduced in Chapter 1, this view can be classified as an everyday preconception. International studies have shown that this idea is particularly frequent among younger children than our study examined, especially in the early primary years (e.g., Brante & Walldén, 2023; Edwards et al., 2018; Mertala, 2019). In Grade 9, this conception was already relatively rare, but still occurred in 3 (10.7%) out of 28 students (Yaghobová, 2021). Taken together with the broader sample in 47 our study (from Grade 4 upward) and findings from international research, this suggests that the prevalence of this idea gradually declines with age and tends to disappear by early adolescence. 

The Internet Exists Beyond the Device 

A large proportion of students demonstrated some awareness that the internet ex-ists “outside” the device, typically referencing home Wi-Fi or general connectivity. In particular, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) reported that 45 (77.6%) out of 58 Grade 4 students and 30 (52.7%) out of 57 Grade 6 students expressed this understanding. However, most were unable to articulate where or how the internet functions beyond their immediate experience. For example, one student noted: 

“[I cannot send a picture] from school, because there is no internet. Like, there is no Wi-Fi [in school], so even if I send it, it is sent only at home [because I have Wi-Fi at home].” 

Grade 4, (Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025) For some students, Wi-Fi functioned less as a technological concept and more as a simple symbol of connectivity—the familiar icon with a dot and radiating arcs at the top of the screen. In this view, more arcs meant “more internet,” but the underlying structure remained ungrasped. Similar findings appear in studies with young children (e.g., Mertala, 2019; Oliemat et al., 2018), where “the internet is something outside the device” was recognized but rarely connected to any network-based understanding. The boundary between online and offline activity was often misunderstood (e.g., Chaudron, 2015; Kumar et al., 2017).

48 The Internet Has a Centralized Architecture 

A common view among students is that the internet has a central point of control or origin, such as a main tower, headquarters, or central computer. This conception, frequently visualised as a single tower or headquarters, is illustrated in Figure 3.1. In Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025), it was reported that 26 (45.6%) out of 57 Grade 6 students held this belief. These central points were often imagined geographically, for example, as one per country or continent. As one Grade 4 student described: 

“[The internet is] in a big tower, eee… in one big tower and the internet goes from there.” 

Although this conception introduces a physical, external location, it remains highly simplified and centralized. In our typology, it is classified as an everyday preconception. This finding aligns with international research documenting persistent beliefs in “a central computer” or “main server” as the origin of online content (Brinda et al., 2018; Papastergiou, 2005). While such views occasionally approach the notion of servers, they generally lack the distributed and decentralized understanding needed for normative accuracy. 

The Internet as a Proto-Network 

In all grades, a substantial proportion of students described, at some point during the interview, the internet as a network that connects devices, but without elaborating on its internal workings. According to Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025), this included 27 (46.6%) out of 58 Grade 4 students, 31 (54.4%) out of 57 Grade 6 students, and 24 (48%) out of 50 Grade 8 students. These views typically stemmed from personal experiences, such as connecting a phone to a friend’s tablet, rather than from a system-level understanding. One student from Grade 5 explained: 

“[Computers are interconnected by] a network … an internet network.” 

Grade 4, (Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025) When probed further, the student could not provide an additional explanation. Although these conceptions introduce the idea of connectivity, they reflect everyday reasoning: students relate familiar devices to one another based on observed interactions, but do not articulate any underlying infrastructure or mechanisms. This type of vague connectivity model is also described in another research (Yaghobová, 2021; Yan, 2005) as a common intermediate step in developing internet understanding. 49 Figure 3.2 Example of student drawings representing an unspecified structure of the internet, redrawn by the author to preserve anonymity. 

The Internet as a Network with Unspecified Structure 

A conception of the internet as a large, global network, often described with vague terms such as “nodes” or “devices,” is frequently reported among students aged 10 to 15 (e.g., Brodsky et al., 2021; Yan, 2005). See Figure 3.2 for one of the student depictions. In the Czech context, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) found this view in 14 (28%) out of 50 Grade 8 students. While students using such terminology appear to move beyond everyday notions, they typically cannot explain how the elements are connected or what roles they play. For example, one student stated: 

“[The internet is] an interconnection of all devices through these nodes,” but when asked to elaborate, responded: “These are probably… through those devices… that it’s connected through that…” 

(Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025) Because this conception introduces non-everyday language without a coherent understanding, it is classified as a scientific preconception in our typology. 

The Internet as a Structured Network, but Incorrect or Incomplete 

A more advanced conception of the internet, involving multiple components and a sense of structure, has been observed among early adolescents across several studies (e.g., Brinda et al., 2018; Papastergiou, 2005). In the Czech context, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) found that 21 (42%) out of 50 Grade 8 students described a multi-step data transfer structure including elements such as routers, towers, and servers, and depicted data as traveling between them (see Figure 3.3 for a typical student representation). However, these descriptions were incomplete or flawed: cables were typically omitted, and towers or satellites 50 Figure 3.3 Example of a student depiction of the internet as a structured, but incorrect, network, redrawn by the author to preserve anonymity. 

were used instead of network routers, with little awareness of their distinct roles. A typical student model might resemble: “Wi-Fi router → tower → server → tower → Wi-Fi router,” with no mention of intermediate routing infrastructure. Because this conception demonstrates a connected view of components and suggests the presence of a structured mental model, it is classified as a mature preconception in our typology. 

The Internet as a Distributed Network with Correct Structure 

Last but not least is a conception that aligns with the instructed model of the internet as a decentralized, global network composed of interconnected servers and routers, with data transferred primarily via cables. This normatively ac-curate understanding was extremely rare across studies; for example, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) documented only two such cases out of 165 participants (1.2%). These students provided accurate descriptions of the internet, identifying routing nodes and transmission media such as fiber-optic cables. According to our typology (see Section 1.1), this represents a mature preconception. An example is the following citation of a Grade 9 student: 

“Well, probably from the phone first to the Wi-Fi router or some kind of receiver, and then either by cable, through a wired network, or through the air to another receiver, and then to some servers where I’m sending the video — and then the same path, just back, to the recipient. Or to the person I’m sending it to, for example.” 

(Yaghobová, 2021) Such high-level conceptions are seldom observed before the age of 11 (e.g., Yaghobová, 2021; Yan, 2005) and mark a shift from intuitive reasoning to a more structured understanding of internet infrastructure (see Figure 3.4 for example). 51 Figure 3.4 Example of student drawings representing the correct architecture of the internet, redrawn by the author to preserve anonymity. 

Overlapping and Developmental Patterns 

Many students transitioned between simpler and more sophisticated models during interviews, or held multiple simultaneously. For example, one student initially described the internet as a centralized structure but later added elements of a networked model. Because students could articulate several conceptions within a single interview, the categories reported earlier are not mutually exclusive, and the summed frequencies therefore exceed the number of participants. These findings support the notion of fragmented and layered understanding, where conceptions do not replace each other but coexist — consistent with the Knowledge in Pieces framework (see Section 1.2 for details). 

3.2.2 The Internet as Function, Place, or Idea: Non-Structural Concep-tions 

While many students described the internet in terms of infrastructure, devices, or physical connections, these structural ideas were often combined with conceptions based on its functions, purposes, or symbolic meaning. Among the youngest learn-ers, however, such functional or symbolic views usually appeared on their own, without any accompanying structural understanding. These non-structural con-ceptions were thus especially common in younger children, but they also persisted in older age groups when structural understanding remained underdeveloped. The following typology outlines key categories found across reviewed studies, typically overlapping with more naive or everyday preconceptions. 

The Internet as Online Activities 

A widespread conception across all age groups was the view of the internet as a set of online actions or possibilities, such as playing games, watching videos, shopping, 52 or chatting. This view was particularly common among younger students and appears to diminish with age. For instance, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) reported that 22 (37.9%) out of 58 Grade 4 students and 21 (36.8%) out of 57 Grade 6 students described the internet in this way, compared to only 8 (16%) out of 50 students in Grade 8. When prompted to describe what the internet is, students often responded in terms of what they do with it: 

“[The internet] is … a thing on which you can do, that you can play videos and look at photos there.” 

Grade 4 This activity-based understanding has also been identified in numerous studies with children aged 3–12 (e.g., Eskelä-Haapanen & Kiili, 2019; Mertala, 2019; Murray & Buchanan, 2018). Such conceptions typically reflect students’ primary engagements with digital media and do not necessarily exclude structural ideas — rather, they provide a familiar experiential anchor. In our typology, these are best understood as everyday preconceptions, grounded in direct usage without reference to underlying infrastructure. 

The Internet as a Place for Information or Content 

Another common view was that the internet is a source or repository of information, often described metaphorically as an encyclopedia, library, storage, or a place “where everything is stored”. In one example, a Grade 9 student stated: 

“Well, I would compare it to a library. … A library has lots of books, and each one is different, and if you tried to read them all at once, you wouldn’t remember any of them, because they contain a huge amount of information, each written by a different author, from different parts of the world, and translated into different languages.” 

(Yaghobová, 2021) This conception has been frequently documented among children aged 6–12 across various studies (e.g., Mertala, 2019; Murray & Buchanan, 2018), and is reflected in the data reported by Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025), where 16 (27.6%) out of 58 Grade 4 students and 21 (36.9%) out of 57 Grade 6 students described the internet in this way, with a comparable proportion still present in Grade 8 (15 students; 30% out of 50). This result is in line with previous data from Yaghobová (2021), where 18 (32.1%) out of 56 participants possessed the same preconception. 53 While such views introduce the notion of information access and storage, they generally do not include technical awareness of how data is routed, stored, or retrieved. As such, this type of conception is classified as an everyday or scientific preconception, depending on the level of specificity and coherence. 

The Internet as a Website or Browser 

Some children, especially in younger grades, equated the internet with a single application or platform, such as Google or a web browser. For instance, one Grade 4 student explained: 

“I imagine the internet … like … it is just Google.” 

(Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025) This simplified view, sometimes overlapping with functional or content-based understandings, has been noted across studies (e.g., Chaudron, 2015), and was observed in 17 (29.3%) out of 58 Grade 4 students, 12 (21.1%) of 57 Grade 6 students, and 9 (18%) of 50 Grade 8 students in the data reported by Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025). Given its reliance on surface-level associations between commonly used apps and the internet itself, this conception is best classified as an everyday preconception. 

The Internet as a Fictitious or Symbolic Place 

Some students described the internet as a non-real or imaginative space, such as a “city of apps,” a factory, or an undefined magical environment; in Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) this view appeared in 18 (31%) out of 58 Grade 4 students,8 (14%) out of 57 Grade 6 students, and 7 (14%) out of Grade 8 students. These metaphorical or fictional conceptions were mostly reported among students aged 8–12 (e.g., Botturi, 2021; Murray & Buchanan, 2018; Yaghobová, 2021) and were often influenced by media representations like Wreck-It Ralph (Disney, 2012) or, in the Czech context, Data Newtown (ČT, 2020). They are classified as everyday preconceptions. 

“Umm, I imagine it like… well, I saw a movie once, and since then I imagine it this way… that it’s like a little town, but an internet one, and it’s inside the computer and so on. And like, when you’re browsing on Google and stuff, it’s like your little character is in that town and walks around, and for example, when you go to YouTube, the character goes to YouTube. And so on.” 

Grade 5, (Yaghobová, 2021) 54 The Internet as Being Everywhere or an Abstract Entity 

In several studies, children also viewed the internet as a global, omnipresent force — “everywhere,” or “in the air”. This conception, noted as early as age 8 (Eskelä-Haapanen & Kiili, 2019; Mai et al., 2022), remained visible across age groups. In Yaghobová (2021), it was identified in 5 (17.8%) out of 28 fifth-graders and 12 (42.8%) out of 28 ninth-graders, showing that this idea can persist even into adolescence. While this view could coexist with more technical knowledge, it often lacked mechanistic detail. In a few cases, children described the internet in anthropomorphic terms (27 out of 165; 16.4%; Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025), for example, as “a brain”. Such views are imaginative but relatively harmless, reflecting an attempt to personify a complex system. Other students characterized the internet as electrical in nature, which can be interpreted as a partially correct intuition, since electricity is indeed fundamental to how digital networks operate. Some even imagined that multiple internets existed (Yaghobová, 2021; Grade 4: 4 out of 28, 14%; Grade 9: 1 out of 28, 3.5%), a preconception that indicates limited differentiation of the internet as a single global network. While anthropomorphic descriptions suggest efforts to reason metaphorically about the internet’s nature, the latter two types represent either partial scientific intuition or a clear misunderstanding. Depending on specificity and coherence, these conceptions are categorized as everyday or scientific preconceptions. 

3.2.3 Data Storage on the Internet 

Students’ conceptions of how data is stored on the internet varied widely, ranging from vague notions rooted in personal experience to more structured views involv-ing servers. Across studies (e.g., Yaghobová, 2021), a developmental progression was observed, with younger children often unaware of physical infrastructure and older students increasingly referring to servers and distributed systems. However, even among adolescents, conceptions were frequently imprecise or incomplete. These patterns are consistent with international research highlighting persistent misconceptions and fragmented knowledge about internet storage systems (e.g., Brinda et al., 2018; Papastergiou, 2005). 

Data Does Not Require Physical Storage 

One common early conception is that data uploaded to the internet does not require any physical storage. Students expressing this idea typically believed that data “stays in the app,” “is on the channel,” or exists “somewhere on the internet” without further clarification. In some instances, data was thought to remain entirely inside the user’s device, or to be “in the cloud” in a purely metaphorical sense. These explanations often lacked any reference to physical infrastructure or external systems. 55 This view was especially common among younger children — for instance, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) reports that 25 (43.1%) out of 58 Grade 4, 18 (31.5%) out of 57 Grade 6, and 17 (34%) out of 50 Grade 8 students demonstrated this belief. Similar ideas have been found across international research: Papastergiou (2005) reported that students aged 12–16 often imagined data stored in modems or satellites, while Hammond and Rogers (2007) found that 10-year-old children frequently referred to storage “inside the device”. Although many students expressed this view at some point during the interview, it was not always their most sophisticated idea; several also demonstrated more advanced conceptions elsewhere in the conversation. Because these views are grounded in direct experience with applications and user interfaces and show no recognition of underlying infrastructure, they are classified as everyday preconceptions. 

Centralized Storage and Proto-Servers 

Another observed conception is that data is stored in a single location, such as “somewhere at Google”. These accounts usually include some idea of a physical location but remain vague about its scale, ownership, and how data is managed or accessed. Students may suggest there is one server per country or continent, or refer to “the main computer” or “headquarters of the internet.” Yaghobová (2021) reports these findings among Czech students, with 18 (32.1%) of students expressing this type of centralized storage view. Papastergiou (2005) likewise found that over a third of 12–16-year-olds believed that web pages are stored in a central computer. Other studies, such as Brinda et al. (2018), suggest that these conceptions might reflect an emerging awareness of server infrastructure, especially when students mention several “central computers” 

but do not yet use formal terminology. Although this preconception introduces the notion of physical infrastructure, it lacks decentralization, redundancy, or any sense of how data flows between components. As such, it is best understood as a scientific preconception in our typology, though in a few borderline cases where students hinted at multiple storage points, it may verge on a mature conception. 

Servers as Storage Points 

In more advanced conceptions, students explicitly mention servers as the place where data is stored or accessed. Some describe servers as special computers that store user-uploaded content or manage data on websites and online platforms. These descriptions vary in clarity: while some students articulate that servers are part of an external infrastructure, others conflate the term with vague ideas such as “somewhere on the internet” or “at the company” .56 Mentions of servers were found in 20 (40%) out of 50 Grade 8 students in Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025), and similar frequencies have been reported in Yaghobová (2021). However, many students learned about servers in everyday contexts — most often through online gaming, where they encounter 

“server addresses” or need to “join a server” . This sometimes results in functional understanding without deeper insight into infrastructure. Because these conceptions vary in sophistication, they are not easy to be correctly classified. When the term server is used without understanding of its role or structure, solely based on everyday experience, for example, as “a place where I play Minecraft” or “something to click on” , it reflects an everyday preconception. If students refer to servers as storage points or use learned terminology without grasping interconnection or distribution, the view is best seen as a scientific preconception. Only in rare cases, such as when students are also holding The Internet as a Distributed Network with Correct Structure preconception (see Section 3.2.1), these conceptions align with a mature preconception. 

3.2.4 Internet Access 

Students’ conceptions of how devices connect to the internet ranged from vague associations with Wi-Fi to more advanced, yet often partial, understandings of networked infrastructure. A variety of access technologies were mentioned across studies, though often without clarity or completeness. As with other dimensions of internet understanding, familiarity tended to arise from personal experience, with deeper conceptual grasp increasing only gradually with age. The following categories describe the most commonly observed conceptions. 

Wi-Fi as Internet Access: From Symbol to System 

Students across grade levels frequently viewed Wi-Fi as synonymous with the internet, often using the terms interchangeably. In younger grades, especially, children treated Wi-Fi as the reason for being online or offline — saying, for instance, they couldn’t send a message “because there’s no Wi-Fi”. Rather than understanding Wi-Fi as a signal or part of a local network, it was perceived as the internet itself or as something that “gives internet”. In Yaghobová (2021), students claimed that “Wi-Fi is an internet” or, conversely, “the internet is a Wi-Fi,” indicating conceptual confusion (7 out of 28 in Grade 5, 25%; 9 out of 28 in Grade 9; 32.1%). Similar findings appear in studies by Mertala (2019) and Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025). Interviewer: “And what’s the difference between Wi-Fi and the internet then? Or are they the same, or is there some difference between them?” 

Grade 5 student: “In my opinion, they’re the same.” 

Interviewer: “Hmm. And do you also know what the difference is 

57 between Wi-Fi and mobile data?” 

Grade 5 student: “Well, mobile data—that’s exactly the same as Wi-Fi, in my opinion.” 

(Yaghobová, 2021) Some students may have initially shown confusion about the concepts at the beginning of the interview, but later answered correctly: Grade 9 student: “Wi-Fi is again wireless—like a completely wireless version of the internet, which is fully adapted for reception by portable devices.” 

Interviewer: “So is Wi-Fi the internet?” 

Grade 9 student: “You could say that Wi-Fi is a form of the internet that is broadcast, for example, by local routers.” 

(later in other part of the interview) Grade 9 student: “Wi-Fi is a way of transmitting the internet, you could say. So yes, Wi-Fi can exist even without the internet.” 

(Yaghobová, 2021) As familiarity with digital environments increased, many students developed a functional, though still incomplete, conception of the Wi-Fi router (often referred to as “the Wi-Fi box”). In Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025), 138 (83.6%) of students across grades ( n = 165 ) recognized the router as a device responsible for internet access. Awareness that the router produces a wireless signal increased with age, being reported by 26 (44.9%) out of 58 fourth-graders, 38 (66.7%) out of 57 sixth-graders, and 38 (76%) out of 50 eighth-graders. However, understanding of how the router connects to the broader internet was much less common: only 9 (15.5%) of students in Grades 4 and 8 (14%) in Grade 6, and 19 (38%) in Grade 8, recognized the role of a cable connection between the home router and the wider external network. 

“Um, Wi-Fi, it’s kind of like, well, just a kind of box that has some sort of, like, sensor inside—I think a satellite sensor, like it receives the signal from the satellite. That’s what Wi-Fi does.” 

Grade 5, (Yaghobová, 2021) Data from Yaghobová (2021) show that 17 (60.7%) out of 28 Grade 5 students and 23 (82.1%) out of 28 Grade 9 students identified the router as part of internet access, but only 7 (25%) of fifth-graders and 14 (50%) of Grade 9 students correctly described Wi-Fi as a signal rather than a device. A more sophisticated distinction that Wi-Fi can connect devices locally even without internet was made by only 3 (5.3%) out of 56 students. 58 Taken together, these conceptions reflect a continuum of understanding. At the everyday level, many students simply associated internet access with the familiar “Wi-Fi box,” sometimes even equating Wi-Fi with the internet itself. With greater experience, some began to distinguish the router’s role more clearly and to identify its key functions, forming what we classify as scientific preconceptions. 

Scientific or Mature Understanding of Local and External Connectivity 

A more advanced preconception involves understanding Wi-Fi as part of a local network infrastructure that connects to the broader internet. Students holding this view described the Wi-Fi router as creating a local area network (LAN), which connects externally via cable or a similar medium. Some were also aware that devices could connect to the router both wirelessly and through Ethernet, and that the router functions as a gateway rather than the source of the internet. This conception was demonstrated by 19 (38%) of 50 Grade 8 students in Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025), with only 6 of them offering more complete models. These six students accurately described both the internal structure of local networks and the router’s role in connecting to the wider internet. Their explanations sometimes included technically relevant details, such as signal limitations or the ability to interconnect devices locally without internet access. Comparable findings have been noted elsewhere, although such conceptions remain rare. For instance, Yaghobová (2021) reported that only 3 (5.3%) out of 56 students knew that Wi-Fi could function independently of internet connectivity, and 10 (17.8%) out of 56 articulated how the router connects to an external network. Because these models incorporate multiple systems and acknowledge both local and global infrastructure, they are best classified as mature preconceptions — albeit ones that are infrequently encountered in the studied age range. 

Other Forms of Internet Access: Hotspots and Mobile Data 

Several studies noted that children were aware of other ways to access the internet, such as via mobile data or shared hotspots, and this awareness is fairly common at an everyday level. However, their grasp of the principles behind these forms of access was noticeably weaker than for Wi-Fi. Some younger children (as early as age 6) were familiar with the idea of turning a mobile phone into a hotspot (Mertala, 2019), and students in Grades 2–3 occasionally referenced cellular data (Eskelä-Haapanen & Kiili, 2019). Yet their accounts rarely included the underlying infrastructure. For example, mobile towers (base transceiver stations, BTS) were almost never mentioned, even among older students (Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025), with only 1 (1.7%) of 58 Grade 4, 2 (3.5%) of 57 Grade 6, and 6 (12%) of 50 Grade 8 students naming BTS. Children often knew that mobile data “uses signal,” but could not describe the source or pathway of that signal. 59 Figure 3.5 Example of a direct transmission conception, redrawn by the author to preserve anonymity. 

This “uses signal” view is highly experiential and thus falls within the category of everyday preconceptions; by contrast, explicit reference to BTS indicates a scientific preconception. 

3.2.5 Data Transfer – How Information Travels Online 

Students’ conceptions of how data travels through the internet ranged from no articulated mechanism (“I don’t know” / “it just appears”), through direct transfer between user devices, to more advanced views involving multiple inter-mediate nodes (e.g., servers and routers). As with other subtopics, conceptions often reflected personal experience rather than a coherent technical model, and understanding generally improved with age. 

Direct Transfer Between Devices 

A common preconception among younger students is that data travels directly between sender and receiver devices without any intermediate components (see Figure 3.5 for example). For instance, a message or image sent via the internet is imagined to “fly” straight from one phone to another. In some cases, this idea was expressed metaphorically (e.g., “little elves carry it through the air”; Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025) or accompanied by complete uncertainty. This direct-transfer view was especially widespread in early grades, with Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) reporting 35 (60.3%) out of 58 Grade 4 students and 28 (49.1%) out of 57 Grade 6 students, but only 12 (24%) out of 50 Grade 8 students holding this belief. Thus, although such notions decline with age, they persist among older learners as well (e.g., Diethelm, Wilken, & Zumbrägel, 2012; Yaghobová, 2021). As in other categories, some students who expressed this view at one point in the interview also demonstrated more complex ideas elsewhere, so this percentage does not imply that it was their only or most advanced conception. An example of this preconception could be the following answer of a ninth-grade student to the task “Please, draw how the chat message will travel from your phone to the phone of your friend”: 60 Figure 3.6 Example of a single-hop transmission conception, redrawn by the author to preserve anonymity. 

“I would draw one phone, a dashed line, and the other phone… showing that the message actually travels along that dashed line and appears on the other one.” 

Because this view omits any conception of infrastructure and relies on naïve or fantastical explanations, it is classified as an everyday preconception. 

Single-Hop Transmission via a Central Device 

A more advanced, yet still incomplete, conception involves a single intermediary device between sender and receiver. Students often envisioned data traveling via a satellite (see Figure 3.6), a broadcasting tower, or a “main point” (sometimes located in the sky or atop a building). For instance, data might be described as following a route like “phone → satellite → phone,” with no recognition of additional network infrastructure. This idea of a single-hop transition was commonly observed in all grades, with Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) reporting it in 67 (40.6%) of all 165 students. Specific types of intermediaries were also mentioned with notable frequencies in the same dataset: 53 (32.1%) out of 165 students referred to a satellite dish or orbital satellite, and 38 (23%) to a tower. These devices were sometimes mistakenly believed to store data. Although this model introduces a node between devices, it lacks the concept of routing or a network path. It is best categorized as a scientific preconception. 

Multi-Hop Transmission—Emerging Network Thinking 

Some students express an understanding that data passes through multiple in-termediate points before reaching its destination. This model, while often vague, indicates a step toward recognizing the distributed nature of internet infrastructure. However, the intermediaries were still often conceptualized as towers, satellites, 61 Figure 3.7 Example of a multi-hop transmission conception, redrawn by the author to preserve anonymity. 

or abstract entities like “a place that checks the data” or “the internet provider” (see Figure 3.7 for an example). This multi-hop idea was observed in a substantial share of students, with Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al. (2025) reporting it in 7 (12.1%) out of Grade 4 students, 14 (24.6%) out of Grade 6 students, and 22 (44%) out of Grade 8 students. Even so, only a small number explicitly referred to routers or switches, and even fewer could explain their function accurately. Just two students (1.2% of the whole sample) in Brom’s sample mentioned a network router (not a Wi-Fi router) as part of the data transmission path. A small number of students displayed what could be called proto-router thinking, recognizing that data takes a complex route without clearly identifying the devices involved (cf. e.g., Diethelm, Wilken, and Zumbrägel, 2012; Lindmeier and Mühling, 2020). This conception falls short of full normative accuracy but signals conceptual progress. These views are best classified as scientific preconceptions, unless they include accurate terminology and explanations of data flow, in which case they are a mature preconception. 

3.2.6 Who Owns the Internet? Conceptions of Ownership 

Although less frequently explored in research, students’ ideas about who owns or controls the internet offer valuable insight into their understanding of digital infrastructure, institutional power, and access. We examined this issue in Study A1.1. Ownership-related conceptions were diverse but typically vague or symbolic, reflecting everyday reasoning more than technical or political understanding. 62 The Internet Belongs to the User or Household 

In Yaghobová (2021), 3 (5.3%) out of 56 students saw the internet as something that belongs to the end user: individual or family. This likely stems from everyday encounters with home Wi-Fi and subscription plans. For instance, one student expressed that the internet “is ours” because it is paid for or installed by their parents. Additional respondents held similar views under the category “each person owns it” (3; 5.3%) or “part of it belongs to everyone, part to me” (1; 1.7%). While this conception lacks a technical basis, it reflects intuitive reasoning based on personal experience and is best categorized as an everyday preconception. 

The Internet Belongs to a Company or Provider 

A more externally focused view, also infrequent but present, was that the internet is owned by large companies such as Google or Apple, or by internet providers. In Yaghobová (2021), 6 students (10.7% out of 56) explicitly named large tech companies as owners, and 2 students (3.5% out of 56) believed that “providers” (unspecified) own the internet. Few went further, attributing ownership to compa-nies that manufacture internet-related devices, such as Wi-Fi routers — a view held by 2 students (3.5% out of 56). These conceptions are best classified as everyday preconceptions. 

The Internet Was Created and Owned by Its Inventor(s) 

Another relatively uncommon conception is that the internet was created and continues to be owned by its original inventors or developers. Students holding this view often personalize the origin of the internet, attributing its existence to a specific (though unnamed) individual or group. While this belief reflects a rudimentary attempt at historical reasoning, it lacks an understanding of the decentralized and collaborative nature of the internet’s development. This conception was reported in the responses of 7 students in Yaghobová (2021) (12.5% out of 56). It is best categorized as an everyday preconception. 

The Internet Belongs to No One 

Some students stated that the internet belongs to no one. This view (7 out of 28 fifth-graders, 25%; 9 out of 28 ninth-graders, 32.1%), found in Yaghobová (2021), may reflect a growing awareness of decentralization, or alternatively a perception of the internet as a public or natural good. While philosophically intriguing, the lack of detail in most such responses limits their classification to scientific preconceptions, unless accompanied by coherent explanations of decentralized architecture. 63 3.2.7 Metaphors Used to Describe the Internet 

In addition to structural and functional models, students often rely on metaphors or intuitive imagery to make sense of the internet. These views offer insight into children’s reasoning but usually lack technical accuracy and decline in prevalence with age. Common metaphors include: • The Internet as an Invisible Substance or Flow : Viewed as something that floats through the air and can be “caught” by special devices or sensors — often likened to wind or light (18 out of 165, 10.9%, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025; 17 out of 56, 30.3%, Yaghobová, 2021). • The Internet as a Generated Resource : Believed to be broadcast from a central source or tower, especially by older children unfamiliar with decentralized infrastructure (32 out of 165, 19.3%, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025; 5 out of 56, 8.9%, Yaghobová, 2021). • The Internet as a Person or Brain : Servers or internet processes are personified (e.g., “the server is like a brain,” or described as little creatures running along wires), reflecting imaginative scaffolding for unseen systems (3 out of 165, 1.8%, Brom, Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, et al., 2025; 2 out of 56, 3.5%, Yaghobová, 2021). • The Internet as a Mail System : In the context of email, some older stu-dents liken the internet to postal services, with addresses and delivery routes (2 out of 56, 3.5%, Yaghobová, 2021). This metaphor can support scientific preconceptions when extended to routing and infrastructure (Diethelm, Wilken, and Zumbrägel, 2012; Hammond and Rogers, 2007; Mumtaz, 2002). These metaphorical conceptions typically reflect everyday preconceptions, though some, such as the mail system analogy, may support transition toward more scientifically grounded views. 

# 3.3 Discussion 

3.3.1 Summary of Key Findings 

This chapter documents a broad spectrum of student conceptions about the internet, ranging from naïve, experience-based ideas to more structured yet still partial understandings. Younger students often viewed the internet as located within a device or equated it with specific functions, such as online activities or accessing content. With increasing age and experience, students more frequently described the internet as a network, but their understanding typically lacked detail about infrastructure, routing, and decentralization. 64 Conceptions of data storage also showed signs of developmental progression. Younger students most often believed that data remained within individual apps or on the device, and when they referred to servers, these explanations were typically grounded in everyday experiences such as online gaming. In contrast, older students were more likely to describe servers in a technically accurate way. Thus, while references to servers appeared across age groups, their interpretation shifted from everyday to more scientific conceptions. Students’ understanding of internet access centered on Wi-Fi, which was sometimes seen as synonymous with the internet. While many learners identified Wi-Fi routers as access devices, they rarely understood how these connect to broader networks, and accurate distinctions between local Wi-Fi and global internet connectivity were uncommon. Nevertheless, some developmental progression was evident: younger students typically described internet access in purely experiential terms (for instance, “having Wi-Fi” meant “having internet”), whereas older students increasingly recognized the Wi-Fi router as a device that connects to an external network, and a few were even aware that a Wi-Fi network can function locally without internet access. These findings suggest a gradual shift from everyday associations between Wi-Fi and connectivity toward more scientific reasoning about the relationship between local and global networks. Regarding data transfer, students frequently imagined direct or single-hop commu-nication between devices. Only a few older students correctly described multi-step routing or mentioned components such as routers or switches. This indicates a limited but emerging awareness of distributed data flow, suggesting that ideas about network infrastructure develop later and remain fragile compared with conceptions of storage or access. Views on internet ownership were highly varied, with some students attributing ownership to users, companies, or inventors, while only a few expressed awareness of its decentralized structure. Such conceptions appear to reflect intuitive social reasoning rather than technical understanding. Finally, metaphorical conceptions were relatively common, especially among younger students. While technically inaccurate, these metaphors reflected intuitive reasoning and occasionally supported the transition toward more scientific ideas. 

3.3.2 Teachers vs. Students: Similar Gaps, Different Language 

While the central focus of this chapter is on students’ conceptions of the internet, understanding teachers’ perspectives is equally important. Teachers play a critical role in shaping students’ ideas, both through the content they choose to present and the implicit assumptions they convey. Yet, teachers’ own conceptions are rarely examined in empirical studies, despite the fact that many are expected to teach complex digital topics without specialized training. To address this gap, our recent study (Brom, Drobná, et al., 2025) examined how teachers transitioning into computer science teaching conceptualize the internet (primary-only, primary-secondary, or secondary teachers; no prior or very little K–9 CS teaching experience, 65 though some had upper-secondary experience). Importantly, almost the same coding scheme as in our Study A1.2 was used, allowing for direct comparison between students and teachers. For the student side, the figures reported here draw on Study A1.1 and Study A1.2 (see Section 3.1.1), which provide the detailed breakdowns across Grades 4, 5, 6, 8, and 9. The dataset in the teacher paper is extensive; here, we use only a subset of results to illustrate some of the contrasts. For interpretive clarity, teachers’ accounts can also be viewed through the Vy-gotskian distinction between everyday and scientific conceptions, which has been widely used in research on conceptual understanding. Although we did not for-mally code teacher data using this typology, their explanations naturally fall along the same developmental continuum: most expressed scientific but not yet fully mature, system-level conceptions. Almost all teachers (94% out of 50) described the internet as a global network, but their conceptions varied considerably in accuracy and detail. Six teachers (12%), mostly at the secondary level, offered a hierarchical model in which the internet was seen as a distributed “network of networks” with servers, routers, backbone routes, and fiber cables as the backbone. Title: Digital systems – computing education after curricular reform Author: Anna Yaghobová Department: Department of Software and Computer Science Education Supervisor: Cyril Brom, Department of Software and Computer Science Education Abstract: Digital technologies shape nearly every aspect of everyday life, yet research-based instructional materials that help lower secondary students under-stand how these technologies actually work remain scarce. While many national curricula, including the Czech one, now emphasise conceptual understanding of digital systems, teachers, especially non-specialists, lack structured, pedagogi-cally grounded resources for topics such as computer architecture and internet infrastructure. This dissertation addresses this gap through four interconnected components. First, it synthesises empirical findings on students’ preconceptions about the internet, drawing on a systematic review, an interview-based master’s thesis by the author, and a mixed-methods intervention study. Second, it exam-ines students’ preconceptions about computers using a parallel methodological approach; this component is presented in the form of a peer-reviewed journal article. Insights from these empirical components directly informed the design of the instructional materials developed in the third and fourth components, both of which are presented as conference papers. These two components introduce and evaluate model lessons on internet principles and on computer principles, designed according to the Evocation–Realization of Meaning–Reflection (ERR) model and anchored in learners’ existing ideas. Across these components, the findings reveal that students typically hold fragmented, experience-based concep-tions, yet these can be substantially reorganised through structured, activity-based instruction. The dissertation proposes a general, preconception-driven design process for creating curriculum-aligned lessons and demonstrates its potential for broader application across the Computer Science curriculum. In today’s increasingly digital world, computer science is no longer just a technical field. It has become a foundational part of modern society. From communication and commerce to healthcare and education, digital technologies influence nearly every aspect of daily life (Castells, 1996; Klopotova & Smirnova, 2022; Paudyal, 2023). While many now view digital competence, the ability to use technology effectively and critically, as a core literacy for the 21st century, comparable to reading or mathematics (Clifford et al., 2020), this competence is incomplete without a conceptual understanding of how digital technologies actually work (Diethelm, Hubwieser, & Klaus, 2012). Concepts such as data handling or networks provide the foundations for reasoning about technology, and these are central to computer science education. This growing focus on understanding, rather than merely using, digital technologies places new demands on schools: they must not only prepare students to use digital tools but also help them understand how these actually work. In response to this growing need, many countries have revised their national curricula to strengthen the role of computer science (European Commission and European Education and Culture Executive Agency, 2022; Falkner et al., 2019; Hubwieser et al., 2015; Tenenberg & McCartney, 2014). These reforms do not merely expand the presence of digital technologies in education; they mark a broader shift from teaching digital tool use toward fostering conceptual under-standing of how these technologies work. This shift is visible across a range of national frameworks, including the CSTA K–12 Computer Science Standards (USA) (CSTA, 2017), the Kerala ICT Curriculum (India) (KITE, 2017), and the National Curriculum in Computing (UK) (Department for Education, 2013). Similar developments can be seen in Finland (Finnish National Agency for Ed-ucation, 2022), Australia (Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, 2021), and Spain (Ministry of Education and Vocational Training, 2021). Even regional initiatives, such as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern’s Informatik und Medienbildung in Germany (Land Mecklenburg-Vorpommern & Tino Hempel Institut, 2019), illustrate how widespread this transformation has become. The Czech Republic is part of this international shift. In 2019, a revised Framework Educational Programme was introduced (MŠMT, 2021), making computer science a compulsory subject in both primary and lower secondary schools. This new curriculum, applicable to Grades 4 to 9 (corresponding to ISCED levels 1 and 2; Eurostat, 2023), has been fully implemented since 2024. 11 The curriculum is organized around four pillars: • Data, Information, and Modelling 

• Algorithmization and Programming 

• Information Systems 

• Digital Technologies 

While curricular reforms in computing education are advancing globally, not all areas of the subject have received equal attention. In classroom practice and research alike, programming and algorithmic thinking have been prioritized, often overshadowing other important domains (Clifford et al., 2020). Topics such as computer architecture, networks, and the underlying principles of digital systems appear far less frequently in instructional materials, particularly at the primary and lower secondary levels. Across the international context, classroom practices that address these topics in a constructivist and pedagogically coherent way remain limited. While resources like Code.org (2025) or Bebras Bebras Challenge (2025) have made significant contributions in areas such as programming or digital citizenship (James et al., 2021), they rarely offer structured support for teaching the principles of operating systems, computer architecture, or the internet at the K–9 level. Although some instructional materials exist for the primary school level in these areas (e.g., Liukas, 2017, 2018; Page & Levine, 2019), resources that address the same digital-technology concepts in a way appropriate for lower secondary students are considerably less common (e.g., Berki & Drábková, 2020; Page et al., 2020; Schiefer et al., 2022). Moreover, materials across both levels often emphasize what digital technologies are used for rather than how they work. Technical content is frequently presented as isolated facts or framed through oversimplified metaphors, which fail to make the underlying infrastructure intelligible to students. This tendency is particularly evident in topics such as hardware or the internet, where instruction often focuses on naming components or describing surface-level functions rather than supporting an understanding of how these technologies are organized and how their elements interact. Even well-developed initiatives such as IT2School (IT2School Projektteam, 2023) provide valuable ideas and activity structures, but they cover only a subset of relevant concepts and remain limited in scope compared to the breadth required by national curricula. Consequently, both internationally and in the Czech Republic, there is a need for materials that are not merely imported from abroad but are explicitly aligned with the Czech curriculum and adapted to the needs of local teachers and students. The shortage of resources for teaching digital technologies corresponds to a similar gap in empirical research. Programming and computational thinking have received considerable scholarly attention, with numerous studies exploring how students understand programming and computational thinking (e.g., Boulay, 1986; Goldman et al., 2008; Hartmann et al., 2024; Putnam et al., 1986; Qian & Lehman, 2017; Sorva, 2012; Swidan et al., 2018; Žanko et al., 2019). In contrast, the didactics of digital technologies, such as computers and the internet, have been 12 researched far less frequently. Existing work tends to focus on older or vocational learners (e.g., Brinda & Braun, 2017; Dechand et al., 2019; Grover et al., 2016), with little emphasis on compulsory schooling, particularly at the K–9 level, which is the focus of this dissertation. Nevertheless, a small but growing body of research has begun to explore students’ prior knowledge about digital technologies (e.g., Mertala & Fagerlund, 2024; Rücker & Pinkwart, 2016), including topics such as data transfer (e.g., Brinda & Braun, 2017), computer architecture (e.g., Pancratz & Diethelm, 2020), or online safety (e.g., Livingstone et al., 2017). While available research suggests that students often hold fragmented ideas about these concepts, there is a notable lack of studies examining how these topics can be addressed in classroom practice. This imbalance is evident in the Czech context as well, especially as regards teacher support. While the pillars Algorithmization and Programming and Data, Information, and Modelling have received considerable attention from publishers and national support platforms (e.g., Berki & Drábková, 2020; Code.org, 2025; Umímeto, 2025), the Digital Technologies pillar, covering topics such as computer architecture, networks, and operating systems, remains comparatively underde-veloped (a similar issue occurs for the pillar Information System , which is out of the present scope). Instructional materials often reduce these topics to factual summaries or isolated lists (e.g., hardware components), with limited conceptual depth and few opportunities for active learning (e.g., Ištok & Hynek, 2022; Roubal, n.d.). In light of the challenges — limited support for teaching digital technologies, gaps in instructional materials, and the lack of research on how to teach these topics in conceptually meaningful ways — this dissertation examines how foundational concepts of digital technologies can be taught effectively in lower secondary schools (ISCED-2, Grades 5-9). It focuses on two areas in particular: the principles of the internet and the principles of the computer. These areas were selected because they are particularly under-represented in existing teaching materials that tend to lack constructivist, student-centered approaches, despite being conceptually important, closely connected to students’ everyday digital experiences, and technically challenging for many non-specialist teachers. The overarching question guiding this work is: 

How can the principles of the internet and the principles of the computer be taught effectively in lower secondary schools (ISCED-2, Grades 5–9)? 

In response to this overarching question, the dissertation pursues two main goals: 1) To gain insight into students’ existing ideas and intuitions related to the selected topics. 2) To design, test, and iteratively refine curriculum-aligned instruc-tional materials that make these abstract concepts more under-standable and teachable , particularly for non-specialist teachers who often face challenges when introducing technically demanding content. 13 These goals are addressed through two interrelated strands of research: (1) the empirical investigation of students’ prior conceptual understanding, and (2) the development of instructional materials that support meaningful and lasting learning. The strands are closely connected: insights from the first strand directly inform the design of lessons and learning activities in the second strand. The classroom evaluation then examines how well these lessons and activities support the development of conceptual understanding. The two key areas within the Digital Technologies pillar of the Czech curriculum, 

Principles of the Internet and Principles of the Computer , are investigated through parallel research strands. Each area is addressed through a dedicated set of research studies that either explore students’ prior knowledge or design curricular interventions (see Table 1). Three of the resulting chapters build on and extend published papers, which are included in the dissertation in their complete form. The topics addressed within each area include the following: • Principles of the Internet – Physical structure of the internet (e.g., the role of servers and routers) – Cookies and digital traces – Types of internet connections – Data transmission • Principles of the Computer – Components and their functions – Operating systems – Files, folders, and data storage The first strand of this research is grounded in the recognition that students do not enter the classroom empty-handed. Their thinking is shaped by everyday experiences, intuition, media exposure, and informal learning. These existing ideas, often referred to as preconceptions , can serve as valuable entry points for instruction, but they are frequently incomplete or based on models from different domains (diSessa, 2018). As a result, students may draw incorrect inferences or apply everyday reasoning in ways that do not align with scientific explanations (diSessa & Sherin, 1998). For example, students may believe that the internet is a single machine located somewhere on the North Pole (Yaghobová, 2021), that computers have a brain (Yaghobová, Drobná, Urban, & Brom, 2025), or that instant messages travel directly from one device to another (Yaghobová, 2021). While such notions may seem harmless, they can distort how new information is interpreted, hinder deeper understanding, and even pose risks in terms of e-safety. The second strand of this dissertation builds directly on these insights.
